as-1.title: Check every input before you use it
as-1.task: Validate every input your app receives against the type, format and length you expect, and reject anything else.
as-1.why: Unchecked input is how attackers inject code or crash your app, which can lead to unauthorised access or an outage.

as-2.title: Use parameterised queries, never string-built ones
as-2.task: Pass user values to the database and to system commands as parameters, for example through an ORM. Never join them into strings.
as-2.why: If user input is joined into a query, an attacker can change what the query does. This can expose or change your data.

as-3.title: Escape output before it reaches the browser
as-3.task: Sanitise or escape every value that you put into an HTML page. The browser then shows it as text and never runs it as code.
as-3.why: Unescaped output lets an attacker run their own script in your users' browsers (cross-site scripting).

as-4.title: Limit repeated sign-in attempts
as-4.task: Rate-limit every sign-in mechanism so repeated attempts are delayed or blocked.
as-4.why: Without limits, attackers can guess passwords at high speed until one works.

as-5.title: Set strong password rules
as-5.task: If you cannot use single sign-on, require long passwords and block weak or commonly used ones.
as-5.why: Short or common passwords are guessed quickly and lead to hijacked accounts.

as-6.title: Store passwords as salted hashes
as-6.task: Store passwords only as salted hashes made with a slow password-hashing scheme, never as plain text.
as-6.why: If your data leaks, attackers cannot read and reuse passwords that are correctly hashed.

as-7.title: Check permissions on every request
as-7.task: On the server, check that the signed-in user may do what each request asks. Use a shared filter or middleware.
as-7.why: Skipping these checks lets one user read or change another user's data.

as-8.title: Keep secrets in a secrets manager
as-8.task: Store passwords, keys and tokens in a secrets manager, never in code or config files.
as-8.why: Secrets in code often leak, and they give attackers direct access to your systems.

as-9.title: Set a Content Security Policy
as-9.task: Send a strict Content Security Policy header that allows only the scripts, styles and images your app needs.
as-9.why: A strict policy stops injected scripts from loading, which limits the damage from cross-site scripting.

as-10.title: Force HTTPS with HSTS
as-10.task: Send an HSTS header with a max age of at least 1 year.
as-10.why: It stops attackers from tricking browsers into an unencrypted connection.

as-11.title: End sessions after a time limit
as-11.task: When a session reaches your time limit, end it or make the user sign in again.
as-11.why: Otherwise, anyone who uses a device with a forgotten open session can act as that user.

as-12.title: Scan uploaded files for malware
as-12.task: Scan every uploaded file for malware before your app processes or shares it.
as-12.why: Uploaded files can carry malware that infects whoever opens them.

as-13.title: Do not show internal details in errors
as-13.task: Show users generic error messages and keep stack traces and version details in your logs.
as-13.why: Debug details help attackers find weaknesses in your app.

as-14.title: Use trusted cryptography libraries
as-14.task: Use well-known, maintained cryptographic libraries instead of writing your own.
as-14.why: Encryption that you write yourself, or that is out of date, often has flaws that you cannot see.

as-15.title: Force a password change after a suspected break-in
as-15.task: Make users change their password when you suspect their account was compromised.
as-15.why: Otherwise an attacker who has the password can stay in the account.

sc-1.title: Keep your code in a central repository
sc-1.task: Keep all your code in one central repository with version history.
sc-1.why: It records who changed what and lets you undo a bad change.

sc-2.title: Require signed commits
sc-2.task: Configure the repository to reject commits that are not signed.
sc-2.why: Signatures make it harder for someone to add changes in a teammate's name.

sc-3.title: Get every change reviewed
sc-3.task: Require review and approval from a designated reviewer before merging to the main branch.
sc-3.why: A second reviewer catches mistakes and malicious changes before they ship.

sc-4.title: Pin your dependency versions
sc-4.task: Pin exact versions of your direct and indirect dependencies in the manifest, and commit the lock file.
sc-4.why: Unpinned versions can change without warning and add bugs or malicious code.

sc-5.title: Build and release the same way every time
sc-5.task: Use one repeatable build and release process that records how each release was built and deployed.
sc-5.why: Releases done by hand are different each time, break more often, and make it hard to know what is running.

sc-6.title: Install only pinned versions when you deploy
sc-6.task: Make your deployment install exactly the versions pinned in your lock file, nothing newer.
sc-6.why: A deploy that takes the latest version can add changes that nobody reviewed.

sc-7.title: Sign your build outputs
sc-7.task: Sign code and container images during the build with a trusted key.
sc-7.why: A signature proves that an artefact is yours and that nobody changed it.

sc-8.title: Verify signatures before deploying
sc-8.task: Verify the signatures of code and images before you deploy or run them.
sc-8.why: It stops changed or fake artefacts from reaching production.

sc-9.title: Share your code inside government
sc-9.task: Share your source code internally so others can review and reuse it.
sc-9.why: Shared code gets more review and avoids duplicated work.

st-1.title: Scan your hosts for vulnerabilities regularly
st-1.task: Run vulnerability scans on your hosts at least every 90 days.
st-1.why: Regular scans find known weaknesses before attackers do.

st-2.title: Watch your cloud settings for mistakes
st-2.task: Scan your cloud configuration continuously to find settings that are wrong.
st-2.why: A single wrong setting, such as a public storage bucket, can expose your data.

st-3.title: Offer a way to report vulnerabilities
st-3.task: Publish a public channel, such as the Government Vulnerability Disclosure Programme, for reporting vulnerabilities.
st-3.why: People outside your team often find problems first. They need a safe way to tell you.

st-4.title: Get your app security-tested every year
st-4.task: Get your app penetration-tested, or put it through a bug bounty, at least every 365 days. An internal or independent team can do it. Keep the report.
st-4.why: Testers find weaknesses that normal reviews miss.

st-5.title: Fix vulnerabilities within the deadlines
st-5.task: Triage every vulnerability and fix it, or formally accept the risk, within the deadline for its severity.
st-5.why: Known weaknesses that nobody fixes are the easiest way into your app.

ns-1.title: Separate public and private network zones
ns-1.task: Place components in separate networks or environments based on how sensitive they are.
ns-1.why: If one part is compromised, separation stops the problem from spreading.

ns-2.title: Restrict access to cloud services outside your network
ns-2.task: Limit who can reach cloud resources that sit outside your virtual network, such as storage and API gateways.
ns-2.why: Open cloud services are a common cause of data leaks.

ns-3.title: Block all network traffic that you do not allow
ns-3.task: Deny all network traffic by default and allow only what is needed.
ns-3.why: Each open path is a way in, so allow as few as you can.

ns-4.title: Keep private network traffic off the internet
ns-4.task: Route traffic between private networks without going over the public internet.
ns-4.why: Traffic over the internet can be intercepted or spoofed.

ns-5.title: Filter traffic coming from the internet
ns-5.task: Filter direct internet traffic to protect against network and application attacks.
ns-5.why: Filtering blocks common attacks before they reach your app.

ns-6.title: Use valid HTTPS certificates
ns-6.task: Make sure certificates come from a trusted authority, match your domain, and are neither expired nor revoked.
ns-6.why: A bad certificate lets attackers intercept the traffic between your users and your app.

ns-7.title: Secure how your services talk to each other
ns-7.task: Make service-to-service calls authenticated, authorised and encrypted.
ns-7.why: If internal calls are not protected, an attacker who gets in can move freely between your services.

ns-8.title: Connect cloud and on-premises systems securely
ns-8.task: Route traffic between on-premises and cloud systems through a secure intermediary.
ns-8.why: Insecure links between environments can expose both.

br-1.title: Back up your important data
br-1.task: Back up important data and systems at least every 7 days and store the backups in a separate, secure place.
br-1.why: Without backups, a failure or an attack can mean permanent data loss.

br-2.title: Test that you can restore from backup
br-2.task: Test your recovery process at least once a year.
br-2.why: A backup that you have not tested may not work when you need it.

br-3.title: Protect backups from being changed or deleted
br-3.task: Make backups impossible to change or delete for 365 days, or as your data retention policy says.
br-3.why: Attackers often delete backups first, so that you cannot recover.

dp-1.title: Keep your data in Singapore
dp-1.task: Keep restricted and classified data in Singapore, in line with the rules for your classification.
dp-1.why: Data stored abroad can break legal and privacy rules.

dp-2.title: Encrypt stored data
dp-2.why: Encryption protects data if disks or backups are stolen.

dp-3.title: Encrypt data as it moves
dp-3.task: Encrypt data whenever it moves between systems or to users.
dp-3.why: Unencrypted traffic can be read or changed on the way.

dp-4.title: Manage your cloud accounts centrally
dp-4.task: Use the central cloud tenant management structure for systems at your classification.
dp-4.why: Central management gives consistent security rules and visibility.

lm-1.title: Store logs away from the system that made them
lm-1.task: Send logs to a different system from the one that generated them.
lm-1.why: Attackers who get in then cannot delete the record of what they did.

lm-2.title: Protect logs from tampering
lm-2.task: Restrict who can read, change or delete logs.
lm-2.why: Tampered logs hide what really happened.

lm-3.title: Log network traffic
lm-3.task: Record the traffic going to and from your network interfaces.
lm-3.why: Traffic logs show suspicious activity you would otherwise miss.

lm-4.title: Log security-relevant events
lm-4.task: Log management and audit events, such as sign-ins and permission changes.
lm-4.why: Without an audit trail, you cannot tell who did what.

lm-5.title: Log database activity
lm-5.why: It shows who touched your data and when.

lm-6.title: Log requests that reach your app from the web
lm-6.task: Log access requests reaching your firewalls, load balancers, proxies and web servers.
lm-6.why: These logs show attacks as they happen.

lm-7.title: Log security events on your hosts
lm-7.task: Log security events on your servers.
lm-7.why: Host logs are key evidence when you investigate an incident.

lm-8.title: Keep security logs for a year
lm-8.task: Keep security logs for at least 365 days.
lm-8.why: Incidents are often found months late, and you need the history to investigate.

lm-9.title: Get alerts about security problems
lm-9.task: Monitor security with automatic alerts, and respond to each alert.
lm-9.why: Alerts let you act in minutes instead of finding a breach weeks later.

lm-10.title: Get alerts on unusual resource use
lm-10.task: Monitor resource usage and alert on abnormal patterns.
lm-10.why: Sudden spikes can mean misuse, such as crypto-mining or an attack.

lm-11.title: Track your service levels
lm-11.task: Monitor and alert on your service-level objectives and indicators.
lm-11.why: You find out about slowdowns before your users complain.

lm-12.title: Send security logs to the central security team
lm-12.task: Centralise security logs and monitoring with the Government Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC).
lm-12.why: The central team can see patterns across government that you cannot see alone.

lm-13.title: Watch for unusual database activity
lm-13.why: Odd queries can be the first sign of data theft.

lm-14.title: Detect and recover from website defacement
lm-14.task: Plan for, detect and recover from defacement of your website.
lm-14.why: A defaced site harms trust, and quick recovery limits the damage.

lm-15.title: Use a structured log format
lm-15.task: Write logs in a consistent, structured format such as JSON.
lm-15.why: Structured logs are much easier to search and analyse.

lm-16.title: Monitor how your app performs for users
lm-16.task: Monitor latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

lm-17.title: Measure how well you deliver software
lm-17.task: Measure and analyse your software delivery performance.
lm-17.why: It shows where your process is slow or error-prone.

lm-19.title: Keep sensitive data out of logs
lm-19.task: Remove or mask classified and sensitive data before it is logged or shared.
lm-19.why: Logs are copied to many places, so secrets in logs leak.

ac-1.title: Give people only the access they need
ac-1.task: Deny access by default and grant each account only the minimum permissions it needs.
ac-1.why: Over-broad access makes any single compromised account far more damaging.

ac-2.title: Require multi-factor sign-in for admins
ac-2.task: Require multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts at sign-in.
ac-2.why: A stolen password alone is then not enough to get into an admin account.

ac-3.title: Remove unused admin accounts
ac-3.task: Disable or remove privileged accounts within 7 days of last authorised use, or after 90 days unused.
ac-3.why: Attackers can use dormant accounts, and often nobody notices.

ac-4.title: Review who has access every year
ac-4.task: Review access at least yearly and remove unneeded access within 7 days.
ac-4.why: People change roles and leave, so access that nobody needs increases over time.

ac-5.title: Use hardened devices for remote admin work
ac-5.task: Require hardened devices for developers and administrators who work remotely.
ac-5.why: A compromised laptop can give an attacker your admin access.

ac-6.title: Change default passwords before first use
ac-6.task: Change default credentials before anything is first used.
ac-6.why: Default passwords are published and tried first by attackers.

ac-7.title: Use Singpass or Corppass for public users
ac-7.task: Use Singpass or Corppass sign-in for services that need a high level of identity assurance.
ac-7.why: It saves effort and gives users a familiar, trusted sign-in.

ac-8.title: Automate removing leavers' access
ac-8.task: Use an account lifecycle tool to automate removal of accounts when people leave.
ac-8.why: Manual processes miss people and leave old accounts open.

ac-9.title: Manage the devices your team uses
ac-9.task: Run an endpoint device management solution for the devices your team uses.
ac-9.why: Unmanaged devices are an easy route for malware and data loss.

ac-10.title: Use identity-based remote access
ac-10.task: Use identity- and device-aware access to private resources instead of plain VPNs.
ac-10.why: It checks who and what connects, not only where the connection comes from.

ac-11.title: Assign each device to one person
ac-11.task: Assign each endpoint device to a single designated user.
ac-11.why: Shared devices make it hard to trace actions and protect data.

ac-12.title: Use single sign-on for internal services
ac-12.task: Use single sign-on for internal services and accounts.
ac-12.why: Fewer passwords means fewer weak or reused ones.

ac-13.title: Rotate long-lived keys and tokens
ac-13.task: Rotate API keys, access keys and tokens every 90 days, or use short-lived ones.
ac-13.why: Old keys are more likely to have leaked.

ac-14.title: Keep a list of all accounts
ac-14.task: Maintain an inventory of all accounts and what each can access.
ac-14.why: You cannot protect or review accounts that you do not know about.

cs-1.title: Pin base container image versions
cs-1.task: Use specific base image tags instead of rolling ones such as latest.

cs-2.title: Use minimal base images
cs-2.task: Build container images from minimal base images.
cs-2.why: Less software in the image means fewer things to attack.

cs-3.title: Pass secrets to containers at run time
cs-3.task: Give secrets to the container when it runs. Never put them into the image when you build it.
cs-3.why: Anyone who has the image can read the secrets in it.

cs-4.title: Do not run containers as root
cs-4.task: Create a non-root user in the image and make it the default user.
cs-4.why: If your app is compromised, a non-root user limits what the attacker can do.

cs-5.title: Lint your Dockerfiles
cs-5.why: Linting catches mistakes and risky settings early.

cs-6.title: Make the container filesystem read-only
cs-6.task: Make the container's root filesystem read-only, except for designated writable locations.
cs-6.why: It stops attackers from changing the running container.

cs-7.title: Scan container images for known vulnerabilities
cs-7.task: Scan images in the container registry for known vulnerabilities.
cs-7.why: It stops you from shipping images with known vulnerabilities.

cs-8.title: Keep images in a private registry
cs-8.task: Host your built images in a private registry.
cs-8.why: Public images expose details about your system.

cs-9.title: Keep the cluster API off the internet
cs-9.task: Disable public internet access to the container orchestrator's API.
cs-9.why: An exposed cluster API gives attackers a direct way into your workloads.

cs-10.title: Separate container workloads
cs-10.task: Isolate container workloads from each other, for example in separate namespaces.
cs-10.why: Isolation keeps an attack inside one workload.

cs-11.title: Detect changes to running containers
cs-11.task: Use runtime protection tools to detect and fix changes to running containers.
cs-11.why: Unexpected changes in a running container often mean an attack.

pm-1.title: Have a plan for cyber incidents
pm-1.task: Have a documented cybersecurity incident plan for your organisation and share it with the team.
pm-1.why: When something goes wrong, a ready plan saves hours.
pm-1.question: Does your organisation already have a cybersecurity incident plan that covers your app?

pm-2.title: Assess the risks before launch
pm-2.task: Document a risk assessment for your app, and get it approved before the first full release.
pm-2.why: It finds risks while they are cheap to fix.
pm-2.question: Has someone written and approved a risk assessment for your app? Who approved it?

pm-3.title: Write your security plan
pm-3.task: Write a plan that describes your app and its protections, and keep it up to date.
pm-3.why: It is the record that reviewers and future teammates rely on.
pm-3.question: Does someone else write the security plan for your app, or do you write it?

pm-4.title: Get leftover risks formally accepted
pm-4.task: Get the remaining risks accepted and approved by the right authority, and review that regularly.
pm-4.why: Someone with authority should own the risks that you cannot remove.
pm-4.question: Who in your organisation should accept the leftover risks for your app? Have they accepted them?

pm-5.title: Submit the approved security plan centrally
pm-5.task: Submit the approved security plan to the central repository.
pm-5.why: It gives government a view of security across all systems.
pm-5.question: Who submits the approved security plan to the central repository? Is it submitted?

pm-6.title: Keep your system documentation up to date
pm-6.task: Keep detailed, current documentation of your app, its architecture and its parts.
pm-6.why: Good documentation is necessary to run and secure your app.
pm-6.question: Is the documentation for your app up to date? Where is it kept?

is-1.title: Install cloud management agents on hosts
is-1.task: Install the cloud provider's management agents on your hosts.
is-1.why: They let you manage configuration remotely and consistently.

is-2.title: Automate security patching
is-2.task: Use automated patch management for operating systems and the software bundled with them.
is-2.why: Missed patches are a top cause of breaches.

is-3.title: Restrict administrator privileges on hosts
is-3.task: Disable remote login for root and administrator users and limit sudo and admin group membership.
is-3.why: Fewer powerful accounts means fewer ways to escalate an attack.

is-4.title: Disable what you do not need
is-4.task: Disable or remove unused functions, ports, protocols, software and services on hosts.
is-4.why: Everything that is running is something an attacker can try.

is-5.title: Harden your hosts
is-5.task: Harden host configuration against an industry standard.

is-6.title: Manage remote administration safely
is-6.task: Use remote administration tools that manage and log remote access.
is-6.why: Audited access reduces misuse and gives you a trail.

is-7.title: Protect hosts against malware
is-7.task: Run anti-malware tools that detect and quarantine malware on hosts.
is-7.why: Malware that you do not detect can steal data for months.

is-8.title: Monitor hosts with an EDR tool
is-8.task: Monitor hosts for threats with an endpoint detection and response (EDR) tool.
is-8.why: It spots attacks that anti-malware misses.

is-9.title: Do not run unsupported software
is-9.task: Make sure deployed software has not reached end of support. If it has, get risk approval.
is-9.why: Unsupported software no longer gets security fixes.

is-10.title: Keep clocks in sync
is-10.task: Synchronise clocks to a common time source.
is-10.why: Out-of-sync clocks make logs useless for investigations.

is-11.title: Register your domain through GovTech
is-11.task: Register .gov.sg and .edu.sg domain names with GovTech as the only registrar.
is-11.why: Properly registered domains are harder to hijack or fake.
is-11.question: Does your app use a .gov.sg or .edu.sg domain, and is it registered with GovTech?

is-12.title: Enable DNSSEC
is-12.task: Enable DNSSEC for your public DNS records and servers.
is-12.why: It stops attackers redirecting users with fake DNS answers.

is-13.title: Register look-alike domains
is-13.task: Register the .sg and common third-level variants of your main domain.
is-13.why: It stops others using similar-looking domains for phishing.

is-14.title: Register your SMS sender ID
is-14.task: Register your SMS Sender IDs, and use only registered IDs for SMS to the public.
is-14.why: It stops scammers spoofing government SMS.
is-14.question: Does your app send SMS to members of the public? If so, is your sender ID registered?

is-15.title: Use only go.gov.sg for short links
is-15.task: Use only the go.gov.sg URL shortener to shorten links.
is-15.why: Official short links tell people a link is genuine.
is-15.question: Does your app share shortened links? If so, do you use go.gov.sg?

sd-1.title: Block secrets from being pushed to the repository
sd-1.task: Configure the repository to reject pushes that contain secrets.
sd-1.why: Secrets pushed to a repository are hard to fully remove and easy to leak.

sd-2.title: Block direct pushes to the main branch
sd-2.task: Configure the repository to prevent pushes, including force pushes, to the default branch.
sd-2.why: Every change then goes through review.

sd-3.title: Require passing tests before merging
sd-3.task: Require continuous integration tests to pass before merging to the default branch.
sd-3.why: It stops broken or unsafe changes reaching main.

sd-4.title: Run static analysis on every change
sd-4.task: Run static analysis in your CI/CD pipeline, and fix or formally accept the real findings before production.
sd-4.why: It finds common vulnerabilities before they ship.

sd-5.title: Scan your dependencies every week
sd-5.task: Scan for vulnerable libraries in your repository at least every 7 days.
sd-5.why: New vulnerabilities in libraries appear constantly.

sd-6.title: Detect secrets in your code
sd-6.task: Detect secrets in the repository automatically, and fix real findings within 1 day.

sd-7.title: Protect secrets used in CI jobs
sd-7.task: Limit CI secrets to protected pipelines and mask them in job logs.
sd-7.why: CI logs and unprotected branches are common leak points.

sd-8.title: Separate production from test environments
sd-8.task: Keep production and non-production environments apart: applications, data, secrets, roles and networks.
sd-8.why: A mistake or breach in test should not affect real data.

ck-1.title: Use standard key-establishment methods
ck-1.task: Use industry-standard key establishment and key derivation methods.

ck-2.title: Rotate encryption keys every year
ck-2.why: Regular rotation limits the damage if a key leaks.
